title: Serving runtime: architecture, kernel scheduling, profiling & runbooks (consolidated)
author: Maya Thompson
body:
Summary
-------
This consolidated reference documents Redwood Inference's serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling policies, profiling and benchmarking playbooks, release notes for recent runtime builds, known issues, and operational runbooks used by the runtime team. It is intended for on-call engineers, performance engineers, and platform owners who operate and evolve the inference runtime.

Scope
-----
- Architecture overview of the runtime components (dispatcher, scheduler, executor, KV cache).
- Kernel scheduling design and configurable policies (latency-first, throughput-first, cost-aware).
- Profiling playbook: how to collect CPU/GPU traces, interpret hotspots, and generate perf regressions.
- Benchmarking suite: standard workloads, metrics, and example runs.
- Release notes: summary of changes since v3.14.
- Known issues and mitigations.
- Runbooks and team wiki pointers (oncall rotations, ownership).

1) Runtime architecture (high level)
----------------------------------
Short intro: Redwood's serving runtime is a modular, GPU-optimized inference engine designed for continuous batching, KV cache reuse, and graceful fallback across model variants. Key components:

- Dispatcher: accepts API requests, normalizes payloads, enforces per-customer quotas and rate limits.
- Router: applies routing policies (region, tier, latency-first) and selects a candidate serving pool.
- Scheduler: groups requests into batches and assigns them to executors using kernel scheduling policies.
- Executor (worker): runs the model kernels on GPU (CUDA/ROCm) or CPU, manages KV cache, and streams token outputs.
- Cache manager: maintains prefix/KV cache entries and coordinates cache hits across executors.
- Telemetry & tracing: per-request traces, token-level metrics, and kernel-level counters.

Design principles:
- Bounded tail latency: prioritize SLOs via scheduling policies and lightweight preemption.
- Cost efficiency: batch size tuning and quantized kernels for throughput-sensitive workloads.
- Observability: deterministic tracing and perf baselines per model variant.

2) Kernel scheduling (concepts & policies)
-----------------------------------------
We separate kernel scheduling from request routing. Scheduler inputs: current queued requests, model variant capabilities, hardware utilization, per-request policy hint (latency|throughput|economy).

Policies (configurable):
- latency-first: minimize p99 token latency. Uses smaller batches, preemption for long-running batches, and reserves small fast workers for latency-sensitive traffic.
- throughput-first: maximize tokens/sec. Aggregates larger batches, favors throughput-optimized kernels (int8/4-bit), and coalesces requests across customers where privacy policy permits.
- cost-aware: optimizes for token cost given a budget constraint; prefers quantized kernels and GPU multiplexing.

Key parameters (config knobs):
- batch_size_max (per model): default 64 for LLaMA-7B style, 256 for LLaMA-70B equivalents on A100-80GB.
- batch_time_budget_ms: how long scheduler will wait to fill a batch (default 8ms latency-first, 30ms throughput-first).
- preemption_grace_ms: time allowed before a long-running batch is preempted (default 20ms).
- reserve_fraction: fraction of workers reserved for latency traffic (e.g., 0.1).

Example scheduler config table (text):
| policy | batch_size_max | batch_time_budget_ms | reserve_fraction | kernel_hint |
| latency-first | 32 | 8 | 0.15 | fused-attn-tile-sm |
| throughput-first | 256 | 30 | 0.00 | int8-optimized |
| cost-aware | 128 | 20 | 0.05 | quantized-gemm |

Scheduling decision flow (simplified):
1. Apply routing policy to select candidate pools.
2. Annotate request with priority and model variant features.
3. Scheduler groups by model variant + max_seq_len + priority.
4. Apply policy-specific batching to form kernel dispatch groups.
5. Assign groups to executors using utilization-aware placement.

3) Profiling playbook (how to collect and interpret traces)
-----------------------------------------------------------
Objectives: localize CPU/GPU hotspots, identify kernel inefficiencies, and provide inputs for regression alerts.

A. Data to collect:
- Kernel timelines (CUDA traces / ROCm traces).
- GPU SM utilization, achieved occupancy, memory throughput.
- Host-side CPU profiles (cProfile/py-spy) for dispatcher and scheduler.
- Runtime counters: queue lengths, batch sizes, KV cache hit rates.
- System metrics: NVLINK/PCIe throughput, GPU memory used, per-device temperature.

B. Tools & commands (examples):
- GPU trace (CUDA): 
  sudo nsys profile --output=trace_{run} --trace=cuda,nvtx,pdk python -m runtime.bench.run --config configs/latency-small.json
- GPU metrics (nvprof deprecated): 
  sudo nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu,utilization.memory,memory.used --format=csv -l 1
- CPU sampling: 
  py-spy record -o profile.svg -- python -m runtime.server.main --work-dir=/tmp/run
- Python line-level: 
  python -m cProfile -o run.prof runtime/server.py && snakeviz run.prof
- Kernel-level perf (for CPU fallback): 
  perf record -F 99 -o perf.data -a -- sleep 30 && perf report -i perf.data

C. Profiling procedure (numbered):
1. Reproduce the workload: use the benchmark harness with representative prompts and sequence lengths (see benchmarking suite below).
2. Run a cold and warm profile to see cache effects (cold: restart worker between runs; warm: back-to-back runs).
3. Collect nvtx annotations and link to traces for kernel start/end mapping.
4. Generate a flamegraph (py-spy or perf) and inspect top 5 hot functions.
5. Correlate spikes in kernel durations with batch sizes and sequence lengths.
6. If long-tail latency is observed, inspect scheduler logs for large batch waits or preemption events.

D. Interpretation guidance (quick):
- High GPU SM utilization but low achieved occupancy -> kernel launch configuration or memory-bound kernel.
- Long host-side times before CUDA launch -> batching or serialization on host; check dispatcher threads.
- Frequent KV cache misses with high token volumes -> consider cache size increase or better sharding policy.

4) Benchmarking suite (standard runs & metrics)
----------------------------------------------
Benchmark goals: measure tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 token latency, GPU utilization, and cost proxy (tokens/sec per GPU-hour) across model variants and kernel configs.

Standard workloads (in bench/configs):
- short-chat: avg prompt 32 tokens, response target 40 tokens (latency-focused).
- long-chat: avg prompt 256 tokens, response target 512 tokens (throughput-focused).
- embeddings-bulk: batch embedding calls with dim=1536.
- regen-stress: repeated reranking and long-context workloads to exercise KV cache.

How to run (example):
- Single-run: 
  ./bench/run_bench.py --model llama-13b-v2 --policy latency-first --workers 8 --duration 600 --output out/llama13b_latency.json
- Cluster-run (k8s job):
  kubectl apply -f bench/k8s/bench-job-llama13b.yaml
  kubectl logs -f job/bench-llama13b

Metrics to capture (JSON schema in bench/out):
- tokens_per_sec (string numeric)
- p50_token_latency_ms
- p95_token_latency_ms
- p99_token_latency_ms
- median_batch_size
- kv_cache_hit_rate
- gpu_utilization_pct

Pass/fail criteria for CI gating:
- Latency-focused models: p95_token_latency_ms <= 80ms, p99_token_latency_ms <= 250ms.
- Throughput-focused models: tokens_per_sec >= baseline * 0.95 and gpu_utilization_pct >= 65%.
- Regression tolerance: no >5% drop in tokens_per_sec relative to baseline for the same commit.

5) Release notes (v3.15-alpha -> v3.15)
-------------------------------------
Recent notable changes (summary):
- v3.15-alpha (2026-02-05): introduced cost-aware scheduling and improved preemption support.
- v3.15-beta (2026-02-18): kernel: fused attention improvements for sequence lengths <1024, default quantized GEMM for int8 backends.
- v3.15 (2026-03-04): stable rollout of latency-first policy default for hosted tier; added KV cache sharding for multi-GPU hosts; fixed memory leak in streaming output path (PR #4123).

Impact notes and rolling guidance:
- v3.15 reduces p95 latency by ~12% for small-chat workload and improves tokens/sec by ~8% for throughput workloads on A100-class hardware.
- Rolling canary plan: enable on 5% of traffic for 48 hours, monitor p95/p99 and error rate; expand to 25% after 24 hours if stable.

6) Known issues (current)
------------------------
- Issue: sporadic p99 spikes with long-seq (>2048) workloads on mixed-generation GPUs.
  - Root cause: kernel tiling fallback that uses suboptimal GEMM path under certain alignment.
  - Mitigation: set environment flag RUNTIME_FORCE_TILING=1 on affected nodes; schedule long-seq traffic to dedicated pools.
- Issue: KV cache eviction thrash under heavy multi-tenant load.
  - Mitigation: increase per-tenant cache quota; enable sticky routing for high-cache-hit tenants.
- Issue: CUDA driver 525.x shows increased per-kernel launch latency on some hosts.
  - Mitigation: pin hosts to 535.x driver for production pools; add CI test for driver version in bench job.

7) Runtime runbooks (operational procedures)
-------------------------------------------
A. High p95/p99 latency incident (step-by-step)
1. Triage: check dashboards -> per-model p95, tokens/sec, queue lengths, average batch size.
2. Isolate traffic: use router filters to shift traffic to second pool (safely redirect 10-20% to warm pool).
3. Collect traces: trigger nsys tracing on a representative worker and capture py-spy on dispatcher for 60s.
4. If KV cache miss rate high (>20% delta): temporarily increase cache retention or route traffic to cache-friendly pool.
5. If GPU utilization low but latency high: check for host-side serialization or network backpressure.
6. Rollback: if recent config change in last 24h, revert using config-rollout CLI: 
   ./tools/config-rollout revert --change-id <id> --namespace serving-runtime
7. Post-incident: open postmortem, link traces and bench results, assign action items.

B. OOM on GPU (executor OOM)
1. Confirm OOM via node logs and nvidia-smi.
2. Drain the node and restart affected runtimes.
3. Temporarily reduce per-process max_seq_len or lower batch_size_max for affected model variant.
4. Patch: update kernel memory estimator and add safety margin (PR template provided in team repo).

C. Degraded throughput (tokens/sec drop)
1. Check scheduler logs for frequent preemption or small batches.
2. Increase batch_time_budget_ms by 10ms for throughput policy; observe effect for 15 minutes.
3. If tokens/sec still low, run bench to compare against baseline and escalate to kernel team.

Runbook templates and escalation contacts:
- Primary oncall: #serving-runtime-oncall (Slack), PagerDuty Seq: eng-runtime-primary -> eng-runtime-secondary.
- Kernel team lead: Daniel Kim (daniel.k@redwood.ai).
- SRE escalation: Priya Singh (priya.s@redwood.ai).

8) Team wiki & ownership
-----------------------
- Owners: serving-runtime (team page), pagerduty rotation and oncall roster are maintained in the team wiki.
- Documentation hub: bench/configs, runtime/configs, and perf-baselines directories in the runtime monorepo.
- Meeting cadence: weekly sync (Wednesdays 10:00 PT) for perf regressions and kernel work.

Appendices
---------
A. Useful CLI snippets
- Collecting nvtx-enabled run:
  CUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=0 NVTX_ENABLE=1 python -m runtime.bench.run --config bench/configs/short-chat.json --output /tmp/trace.json
- Quick baseline run for CI:
  ./bench/run_bench.py --model gorilla-6b --policy latency-first --duration 120 --output /tmp/ci_gorilla.json

B. Where to find artifacts
- Benchmark results: s3://redwood-perf/bench/out/{date}/{commit}.json
- Traces: s3://redwood-perf/traces/{run_id}.nsys
- Perf dashboards: Grafana -> "Serving Runtime / Performance"

C. Next planned work (roadmap items)
- Per-tenant adaptive batching (Q2 2026).
- Kernel autotuner: runtime selects tile sizes and launch configs per-host (prototype Q3 2026).
- Better KV cache coherence for multi-GPU hosts (Q3 2026).

If you have corrections, please edit this page and ping the reviewers list.
